title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered maximum_model_calls for independent per‑arm generation = 400). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial injection budgeting, and model‑call accounting) for informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived (execution/*, analysis/*).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) offers operator productivity gains for network operations (NetOps) but raises operational safety risks: an incorrect or ill‑timed change can break reachability, violate policy, or cause outages. The NetOps community has therefore proposed tool‑grounding, deterministic validators, and generate–validate–repair architectures to improve correctness and reduce hallucination‑driven errors. To move beyond design claims and small prototypes, we preregistered a workflow‑centred, paired experiment to quantify whether deterministic verifier augmentation reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals under both benign and adversarial prompts.

This manuscript reports the complete preregistered execution (study_id = cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1), the deterministic archival artifacts, a data‑driven diagnosis of why the confirmatory hypothesis was non‑informative in this run, and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations to make future repeats informative. The primary research question from the preregistration was: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic validator → optional repair) change the rate of unsafe network‑change proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts? Our contributions are (1) the full, preregistered paired experiment and deterministic archives for N=200 tasks; (2) a reproducible, artifact‑grounded diagnosis of the ceiling/testability failure observed when shared generation semantics and a zero baseline unsafe rate coincide; and (3) practical, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial injection targeting baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15%, and exploratory reserve usage) for informative confirmatory repeats.
sections.related_work:
LLMs are rapidly being applied to NetOps tasks such as intent translation, configuration synthesis, and automated remediation; surveys and prototype reports document architectures combining LLMs with deterministic tools and verifiers to improve task correctness [arXiv:2605.12729; SSRN:7132138; IEEE OJCOMS 2026]. Generate–validate–repair and divide–verify–refine pipelines have been shown to reduce constraint violations in experimental settings, but effect sizes and external validity depend on verifier fidelity, generation semantics, and prompt design [openalex:W4412888330; openalex:W7161354925]. Red‑teaming and guardrail literatures highlight trade‑offs between false refusals and unblocked unsafe proposals and recommend workflow‑centred, replayable evaluations that include deterministic sandboxing and archived scoring traces [TechRxiv:177004277; TechRxiv:177006109].

Our study is positioned as a methodological, workflow‑centred contribution: rather than proposing a new verification algorithm, we publish a fully preregistered confirmatory run with deterministic artifacts and analyze how execution choices (shared vs independent generation) and budgeting interact with statistical estimands. This complements prior prototype and position papers by providing a reproducible example of how an otherwise well‑specified preregistration can become non‑informative due to execution semantics.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1). The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (SAFE encoded as 1). The design was a paired binary comparison with N=200 unique tasks paired across two pipelines, using an exact McNemar two‑sided test implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10000 resamples with seed = 1729.

Task generation and sampling plan. A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks using a preregistered RNG schedule (seed sequence starting with preregistered seed = 42 and per‑task seeds 1..200). Tasks targeted operationally meaningful changes limited to admin/mtu/vlan fields across multi‑device single‑AS topologies (task manifest archived at execution/task_manifest.jsonl). The sampling plan split tasks into benign and adversarial clusters; adversarial prompts followed preregistered templated obfuscation/negation transforms intended to increase the baseline unsafe rate. The preregistration explicitly recorded the allowed generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation or shared_initial_candidate (shared generation). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false) as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json.

Pipelines, validators, and repairs. Two pipelines were compared: baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (LLM candidate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional single repair). deterministic_netops_validator_v5 executed in a deterministic sandbox and applied full_intent_constraint_validation to label candidates SAFE/UNSAFE and produce detailed validation_before/after traces. For the confirmatory episodes no automatic repairs were applied (repair_provider_trace = null in scoring JSONs). Scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) include normalized_configuration, parsed command counts, violation lists, and validator verdicts; these artifacts were the basis for binary outcome coding.

Generation semantics and budget. The preregistration allowed independent per‑arm generation (two LLM calls per pair) or shared_initial_candidate (one shared LLM call per pair). Independent generation permits genuine per‑arm variability and is required for standard paired causal contrasts because it lets the guarded arm be exposed to a different generation than baseline. The executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics and therefore performed a single LLM generation per task. Model accounting in execution/execution_manifest.json records model_calls_used = 200 while the preregistered maximum_model_calls for independent per‑arm generation would have been 400; this difference is central to the testability diagnosis.

Analysis procedures and handling of missingness. The primary analysis was executed by paired_binary_analysis_v1. Each pair produced two binary outcomes (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE) from the deterministic validator; the analysis produced the 2×2 contingency table (n11, n10, n01, n00), exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value, and paired bootstrap percentile CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Preregistered missingness rules permitted one automatic retry for failed model calls, replacement for contaminated tasks, and an abort/downgrade if technical failures exceeded 10% of pairs. Execution produced no technical failures or exclusions; missingness_summary and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts confirm successful complete_pair_count = 200.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The experiment completed planned_episode_count = 400 (200 paired tasks × 2 pipeline scorings derived from a single shared initial generation per task) with failed_episode_count = 0 and model_calls_used = 200 (execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json). The executed shared generation semantics are recorded in model_configuration.json (independent_condition_generation = false) and in provider_call_audit entries in deterministic_reconciliation.json.

Primary outcomes. The analysis condition summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv) reports baseline SAFE successes = 200/200 and guarded SAFE successes = 200/200 (SAFE encoded as 1), yielding observed SAFE rates of 1.0 in both arms. The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). These numeric outputs come directly from analysis/results.json and the CSV artifacts.

Representative diagnostics. Scoring JSON examples (execution/scoring/task-000001‑*.json, task-000002‑*.json, task-000003‑*.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate content in baseline and guarded arms and validator traces reporting violation_count = 0 (valid = true) in validation_before and validation_after blocks. No repair_provider_trace entries are present for the confirmatory episodes, confirming the guarded pipeline did not apply automatic repairs in these examples. The deterministic_reconciliation.json artifact confirms consistent episode accounting (complete_pair_count = 200; hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; all deterministic checks passed).

Sensitivity and exploratory reserves. The preregistration reserved up to 50 exploratory tasks to estimate verifier ROC and refusal characteristics; this exploratory reserve was not used in confirmatory hypothesis testing here. The preregistered sensitivity analyses (treating technical failures as safe or unsafe) were unnecessary because no technical failures occurred; analysis/missingness_summary.csv records zero failed episodes.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded diagnosis of a non‑informative confirmatory test. The confirmatory test required discordant pairs (n10 or n01) to measure verifier effect. Three archive‑verifiable facts combined to produce a ceiling/testability failure in this execution:

1) Shared initial generation: independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate) produced identical LLM candidates for baseline and guarded arms. The canonical per‑pair LLM output was stored at execution/responses/task‑<id>‑shared‑initial.txt and reused across arms; provider_call_audit shows a single shared_initial_generation per pair (deterministic_reconciliation.json).

2) Zero baseline unsafe rate: for the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and the sampled tasks, generated candidates satisfied the deterministic validator so the baseline unsafe rate was 0.0 (baseline SAFE = 200/200; analysis/condition_summary.csv).

3) Budgeting trade‑off: executing shared generation required only 200 LLM calls instead of the preregistered 400 for independent per‑arm generation. The executed model_calls_used = 200 versus the preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 (execution/execution_manifest.json), and this choice directly constrained the ability to create per‑arm variability.

When a shared candidate is SAFE under the validator, the guarded arm (which validates the same candidate) cannot produce a discordant SAFE→UNSAFE or UNSAFE→SAFE outcome absent a repair that changes the candidate; because no repairs were applied in confirmatory episodes, all pairs were concordant (n11), leading to p = 1.0 and CI collapsed to [0.0, 0.0]. This is a classic testability/ceiling failure for paired designs that rely on per‑arm variability.

Practical, artifact‑grounded recommendations for informative repeats. All recommendations below follow directly from the preregistration and execution accounting artifacts and are intended to be implementable without inventing new tooling.

(1) Independent per‑arm generation for paired causal contrasts. For N=200 pairs, independent generation implies ≈200 additional model calls (preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 vs executed 200). If the objective is to measure verifier causal impact with McNemar inference, independent per‑arm calls should be the default.

(2) Calibrated adversarial injection to ensure nonzero baseline unsafe rate. The preregistered power plan assumed baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15% and a detectable paired reduction of ≈7 percentage points. To achieve that operating point, preregister an adversarial injection fraction or stronger adversarial transformations so baseline unsafe rates under the target model are nonzero and aligned with power assumptions.

(3) Use the exploratory reserve to estimate verifier ROC and refusal trade‑offs. Reserve and run the preregistered exploratory sample (up to 50 tasks) to estimate verifier true/false positive rates before confirmatory testing; record these ROC estimates and CIs in archived artifacts.

(4) Report model‑call accounting and make budget trade‑offs explicit in preregistration. The exact executed model_calls_used and the preregistered maximum_model_calls are archived and should be reported in any repeat to permit reproducible interpretation of design choices.

(5) Where possible, run a small multi‑model panel to assess generality; if budget is constrained, prioritize independent per‑arm draws over wide model sampling because paired contrasts require per‑arm variability.

Operational implications and authoritative framing. This run does not provide evidence that verifiers are unnecessary, nor does it prove verifier efficacy. Instead, it is a reproducible demonstration that preregistered paired contrasts can become untestable if generation semantics and budgeting choices eliminate per‑arm variability or if baseline unsafe rates are zero. The scientific contribution is therefore methodological: we publish a complete, deterministic artifact bundle (execution/*, analysis/*) and operational evidence of how specific execution semantics invalidate a preregistered paired estimand.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. The value of this work is reproducibility and methodological: (1) we publish a complete preregistered run with deterministic artifacts that permit exact replay; (2) we provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) we provide concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial budgeting to target baseline unsafe rates ≈10–15%, and exploratory ROC estimation) to design informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the supplied bundle (execution/*, analysis/*) to support deterministic replays and community replication.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
